effect_mechanism: Restoration of degraded wetlands recovers species and communities.
conditionality: Recovery depends strongly on the organism group; synthesis calls recovery excellent (graded strong).
justification: Meli et al. (2014). Restoration Enhances Wetland Biodiversity and Ecosystem Service Supply, but Results Are Context-Dependent: A Meta-Analysis. PLoS ONE. — p.1: "Biodiversity showed excellent recovery, though the precise recovery depended strongly on the type of organisms involved."

effect_mechanism: Created and restored wetlands remove nitrogen and phosphorus from runoff and wastewater passing through them.
conditionality: Removal depends on loading rate, temperature and area; restored wetlands on former farmland were less efficient for phosphorus. Mostly Europe and North America. Graded on the percent band (37%, 46% > 30%).
justification: Land et al. (2016). How effective are created or restored freshwater wetlands for nitrogen and phosphorus removal? A systematic review. Environmental Evidence. — p.1: "Removal efficiency for TN was significantly correlated with hydrologic loading rate (HLR) and T, and the median was 37 %, with a 95 % confidence interval of 29–44 %. Removal efficiency for TP was significantly correlated with inlet TP concentration, HLR, T, and A. Median TP removal efficiency was 46 % with a 95 % confidence interval of 37–55 %." | p.1: "Conclusions: On average, created and restored wetlands significantly reduce the transport of TN and TP in treated wastewater and urban and agricultural runoff, and may thus be effective in efforts to counteract eutrophication. However, restored wetlands on former farmland were significantly less efficient than other wetlands at TP removal."

effect_mechanism: Wetland storage lowers flood frequency and peak size.
conditionality: Existing wetlands, not restoration; medium pooled effect with large unexplained variation.
justification: Kadykalo et al. (2016). The flow regulation services of wetlands. Ecosystem Services. — p.1: "We found that, consistent with conventional wisdom, on average wet- lands reduce the frequency and magnitude of ﬂoods and increase ﬂood return period; augment low ﬂows; and decrease runoff and streamﬂow." | p.4: "Fifty-nine weighted effect sizes were calculated from the 28 stu- dies, yielding a medium positive mean effect size"

effect_mechanism: Floodplain wetlands store floodwater; upland wetlands generate runoff.
conditionality: Direction depends on wetland type and position in the catchment.
justification: Acreman et al. (2013). How Wetlands Affect Floods. Wetlands. — p.2: "Upland wetlands generally tend to be flood generating areas while floodplain wetlands have a greater potential to reduce floods."

effect_mechanism: Wetlands raise low flows but lower total runoff and streamflow.
conditionality: Both directions stated in the same conclusion: more dry-season baseflow, less total water yield.
justification: Kadykalo et al. (2016). The flow regulation services of wetlands. Ecosystem Services. — p.1: "We found that, consistent with conventional wisdom, on average wet- lands reduce the frequency and magnitude of ﬂoods and increase ﬂood return period; augment low ﬂows; and decrease runoff and streamﬂow."

effect_mechanism: Rewetting drained organic soils cuts CO2 and N2O emissions and can turn the site into a net greenhouse-gas sink.
conditionality: Methane emissions rise after rewetting; the net climate effect depends on the balance. Avoided emissions, not only new sequestration.
justification: IPCC (2014). 2013 Supplement to the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories: Wetlands. Chapter 3 Rewetted Organic Soils; Chapter 4 Coastal Wetlands / Inland Wetland Mineral Soils (chapter as applicable). IPCC, Switzerland. — p.24: "Rewetting inland organic soils raises the water table again, decreases CO2 emissions, rapidly decreases N2O emissions to almost zero, and increases CH4 emissions compared to the drained state, as the oxygen level in the soil drops and methanogenesis starts again. Rewetting can also restore wetlands to a state where net CO2 emissions are greatly reduced or even become negative, causing the wetlands to function as a net remover of greenhouse gases from the atmosphere"

effect_mechanism: Rewetting arable peat replaces arable cropping with grazing and other uses.
conditionality: One high-income case (Wicken Fen, UK) reported inside the synthesis; society-level net benefit was positive but arable food production fell sharply.
justification: Ramsar Convention on Wetlands (2025). Global Wetland Outlook 2025: Valuing, conserving, restoring and financing wetlands. Secretariat of the Convention on Wetlands, Gland. — p.38: "The restored wetland provided increased climate mitigation, flood regulation, livestock grazing and recreational value, but there was a large loss of arable food production."

effect_mechanism: Benefits shift from local farmers (arable income) to distant visitors and society (recreation, climate).
conditionality: Same single high-income case; a shift in who benefits, not a measured income change. Graded slight.
justification: Ramsar Convention on Wetlands (2025). Global Wetland Outlook 2025: Valuing, conserving, restoring and financing wetlands. Secretariat of the Convention on Wetlands, Gland. — p.39: "The economic benefits from the food provision service provided by the arable farming largely accrued to a small number of local farmers. Conversely, the recreational value of the restored wetland accrued to a much larger number of more distantly located and urban residents"
